strengths: Structural conservation guarantee via Proposition 1 is elegant and rigorously proven; conservation errors reach machine precision (~10^-8), a clear practical advantage over soft-constraint methods
Comprehensive theoretical framework with hard lower-bound guarantees (L-head) and effective dual-bound control via DCL (D-head); clear proofs in appendix
Thorough experimental validation across four diverse benchmarks (convection-diffusion, shallow water, traffic flow, spinodal decomposition) spanning different physics and constraint types
Strong empirical results: 17.3× speedup on spinodal decomposition, 67% reduction in shallow water depth MAE vs projection baselines, preservation of microstructural statistics beyond training horizon

Rigorous design validation through extensive ablations (Tables 6-7) demonstrating importance of each component; ERF analysis (Figures 4, 12-13) convincingly shows learned operators are genuinely local
Honest limitations discussion and transparent reporting of D-head violations as first-class metrics rather than hiding shortcomings; excellent scientific integrity
Clear presentation with logical flow; comprehensive appendix with complete proofs, experimental details, and supplementary visualizations
Configurable stencil radius enables large timesteps with localized effective receptive fields, achieving practical speedups while maintaining physical interpretation
weaknesses: D-head for dual-bounded quantities lacks strict theoretical guarantees; averaging Eq. (3) between outflow and inflow branches breaks both hard constraints, relying instead on empirical Dual Consistency Loss regularization (~0.5-7% violation rates). No convergence analysis provided for why DCL training works

Severe scope limitations: guarantees hold only for periodic boundary conditions (Dirichlet/Neumann/mixed BCs require unspecified 'careful treatment'); restricted to source-free conservation laws; limited to regular grids, excluding unstructured meshes and adaptive refinement—critical for modern scientific computing applications

No direct experimental comparison to FINN (Praditia et al., 2021), the most closely related flux-based method, making it difficult to assess the actual advantage of the proposed approach over existing flux-based surrogates

Incremental methodological novelty: flux-based conservation is established; main contributions are specific parameterizations (L/U/D-heads) and stencil channelization from LBM. While integration is sensible, the advance is evolutionary rather than revolutionary

Practical limitations: stencil radius must be manually tuned for each timestep (Table 5 shows different radii needed for different ∆t values); no principled or adaptive mechanism provided. Task-specific FluxNet-LAP for shallow water (momentum decomposition with h² pressure gating) introduces manually-designed physics, somewhat contradicting the generic framework claim

Small datasets for some benchmarks: 100 training trajectories for traffic flow; single long trajectory for spinodal decomposition using one-shot learning paradigm. Generalization to larger, more diverse datasets or harder problems unclear
Limited analysis of failure modes, hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., DCL weight γ), or performance on problems with strong nonlinearities beyond traffic flow shocks
Number of random seeds for error bars not explicitly stated; no explicit code availability statement limiting reproducibility despite detailed documentation
